To Sherlock Holmes she is always _the_ woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

“My dear fellow,” said Sherlock Holmes as we sat on either side of the fire in his lodgings at Baker Street, “life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence. If we could fly out of that window hand in hand, hover over this great city, gently remove the roofs, and peep in at the queer things which are going on, the strange coincidences, the plannings, the cross-purposes, the wonderful chains of events, working through generations, and leading to the most _outré_ results, it would make all fiction with its conventionalities and foreseen conclusions most stale and unprofitable.”

“And yet I am not convinced of it,” I answered. “The cases which come to light in the papers are, as a rule, bald enough, and vulgar enough. We have in our police reports realism pushed to its extreme limits, and yet the result is, it must be confessed, neither fascinating nor artistic.”

“A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect,” remarked Holmes. “This is wanting in the police report, where more stress is laid, perhaps, upon the platitudes of the magistrate than upon the details, which to an observer contain the vital essence of the whole matter. Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.”

I smiled and shook my head. “I can quite understand your thinking so,” I said. “Of course, in your position of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled, throughout three continents, you are brought in contact with all that is strange and bizarre. But here”—I picked up the morning paper from the ground—“let us put it to a practical test. Here is the first heading upon which I come. ‘A husband’s cruelty to his wife.’ There is half a column of print, but I know without reading it that it is all perfectly familiar to me. There is, of course, the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, the sympathetic sister or landlady. The crudest of writers could invent nothing more crude.”

“Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument,” said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. “This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.”

He held out his snuffbox of old gold, with a great amethyst in the centre of the lid. Its splendour was in such contrast to his homely ways and simple life that I could not help commenting upon it.

When I glance over my notes and records of the Sherlock Holmes cases between the years ’82 and ’90, I am faced by so many which present strange and interesting features that it is no easy matter to know which to choose and which to leave. Some, however, have already gained publicity through the papers, and others have not offered a field for those peculiar qualities which my friend possessed in so high a degree, and which it is the object of these papers to illustrate. Some, too, have baffled his analytical skill, and would be, as narratives, beginnings without an ending, while others have been but partially cleared up, and have their explanations founded rather upon conjecture and surmise than on that absolute logical proof which was so dear to him. There is, however, one of these last which was so remarkable in its details and so startling in its results that I am tempted to give some account of it in spite of the fact that there are points in connection with it which never have been, and probably never will be, entirely cleared up.

The year ’87 furnished us with a long series of cases of greater or less interest, of which I retain the records. Among my headings under this one twelve months I find an account of the adventure of the Paradol Chamber, of the Amateur Mendicant Society, who held a luxurious club in the lower vault of a furniture warehouse, of the facts connected with the loss of the British barque _Sophy Anderson_, of the singular adventures of the Grice Patersons in the island of Uffa, and finally of the Camberwell poisoning case. In the latter, as may be remembered, Sherlock Holmes was able, by winding up the dead man’s watch, to prove that it had been wound up two hours before, and that therefore the deceased had gone to bed within that time—a deduction which was of the greatest importance in clearing up the case. All these I may sketch out at some future date, but none of them present such singular features as the strange train of circumstances which I have now taken up my pen to describe.

It was in the latter days of September, and the equinoctial gales had set in with exceptional violence. All day the wind had screamed and the rain had beaten against the windows, so that even here in the heart of great, hand-made London we were forced to raise our minds for the instant from the routine of life and to recognise the presence of those great elemental forces which shriek at mankind through the bars of his civilisation, like untamed beasts in a cage. As evening drew in, the storm grew higher and louder, and the wind cried and sobbed like a child in the chimney. Sherlock Holmes sat moodily at one side of the fireplace cross-indexing his records of crime, while I at the other was deep in one of Clark Russell’s fine sea-stories until the howl of the gale from without seemed to blend with the text, and the splash of the rain to lengthen out into the long swash of the sea waves. My wife was on a visit to her mother’s, and for a few days I was a dweller once more in my old quarters at Baker Street.

heldout.text:
I had called upon my friend, Mr. Sherlock Holmes, one day in the autumn of last year and found him in deep conversation with a very stout, florid-faced, elderly gentleman with fiery red hair. With an apology for my intrusion, I was about to withdraw when Holmes pulled me abruptly into the room and closed the door behind me.

“You could not possibly have come at a better time, my dear Watson,” he said cordially.

“Then I can wait in the next room.”

“Not at all. This gentleman, Mr. Wilson, has been my partner and helper in many of my most successful cases, and I have no doubt that he will be of the utmost use to me in yours also.”

The stout gentleman half rose from his chair and gave a bob of greeting, with a quick little questioning glance from his small fat-encircled eyes.

“Try the settee,” said Holmes, relapsing into his armchair and putting his fingertips together, as was his custom when in judicial moods. “I know, my dear Watson, that you share my love of all that is bizarre and outside the conventions and humdrum routine of everyday life. You have shown your relish for it by the enthusiasm which has prompted you to chronicle, and, if you will excuse my saying so, somewhat to embellish so many of my own little adventures.”

“Your cases have indeed been of the greatest interest to me,” I observed.

“You will remember that I remarked the other day, just before we went into the very simple problem presented by Miss Mary Sutherland, that for strange effects and extraordinary combinations we must go to life itself, which is always far more daring than any effort of the imagination.”

“A proposition which I took the liberty of doubting.”

“You did, Doctor, but none the less you must come round to my view, for otherwise I shall keep on piling fact upon fact on you until your reason breaks down under them and acknowledges me to be right. Now, Mr. Jabez Wilson here has been good enough to call upon me this morning, and to begin a narrative which promises to be one of the most singular which I have listened to for some time. You have heard me remark that the strangest and most unique things are very often connected not with the larger but with the smaller crimes, and occasionally, indeed, where there is room for doubt whether any positive crime has been committed. As far as I have heard, it is impossible for me to say whether the present case is an instance of crime or not, but the course of events is certainly among the most singular that I have ever listened to. Perhaps, Mr. Wilson, you would have the great kindness to recommence your narrative. I ask you not merely because my friend Dr. Watson has not heard the opening part but also because the peculiar nature of the story makes me anxious to have every possible detail from your lips. As a rule, when I have heard some slight indication of the course of events, I am able to guide myself by the thousands of other similar cases which occur to my memory. In the present instance I am forced to admit that the facts are, to the best of my belief, unique.”

We were seated at breakfast one morning, my wife and I, when the maid brought in a telegram. It was from Sherlock Holmes and ran in this way:

“Have you a couple of days to spare? Have just been wired for from the west of England in connection with Boscombe Valley tragedy. Shall be glad if you will come with me. Air and scenery perfect. Leave Paddington by the 11:15.”

“What do you say, dear?” said my wife, looking across at me. “Will you go?”

“I really don’t know what to say. I have a fairly long list at present.”

“Oh, Anstruther would do your work for you. You have been looking a little pale lately. I think that the change would do you good, and you are always so interested in Mr. Sherlock Holmes’ cases.”

“I should be ungrateful if I were not, seeing what I gained through one of them,” I answered. “But if I am to go, I must pack at once, for I have only half an hour.”

My experience of camp life in Afghanistan had at least had the effect of making me a prompt and ready traveller. My wants were few and simple, so that in less than the time stated I was in a cab with my valise, rattling away to Paddington Station. Sherlock Holmes was pacing up and down the platform, his tall, gaunt figure made even gaunter and taller by his long grey travelling-cloak and close-fitting cloth cap.

“It is really very good of you to come, Watson,” said he. “It makes a considerable difference to me, having someone with me on whom I can thoroughly rely. Local aid is always either worthless or else biassed. If you will keep the two corner seats I shall get the tickets.”

We had the carriage to ourselves save for an immense litter of papers which Holmes had brought with him. Among these he rummaged and read, with intervals of note-taking and of meditation, until we were past Reading. Then he suddenly rolled them all into a gigantic ball and tossed them up onto the rack.

“Have you heard anything of the case?” he asked.

“Not a word. I have not seen a paper for some days.”

“The London press has not had very full accounts. I have just been looking through all the recent papers in order to master the particulars. It seems, from what I gather, to be one of those simple cases which are so extremely difficult.”

“But it is profoundly true. Singularity is almost invariably a clue. The more featureless and commonplace a crime is, the more difficult it is to bring it home. In this case, however, they have established a very serious case against the son of the murdered man.”

“Well, it is conjectured to be so. I shall take nothing for granted until I have the opportunity of looking personally into it. I will explain the state of things to you, as far as I have been able to understand it, in a very few words.

heldout.story: VI. THE MAN WITH THE TWISTED LIP
heldout.text:
Isa Whitney, brother of the late Elias Whitney, D.D., Principal of the Theological College of St. George’s, was much addicted to opium. The habit grew upon him, as I understand, from some foolish freak when he was at college; for having read De Quincey’s description of his dreams and sensations, he had drenched his tobacco with laudanum in an attempt to produce the same effects. He found, as so many more have done, that the practice is easier to attain than to get rid of, and for many years he continued to be a slave to the drug, an object of mingled horror and pity to his friends and relatives. I can see him now, with yellow, pasty face, drooping lids, and pin-point pupils, all huddled in a chair, the wreck and ruin of a noble man.

One night—it was in June, ’89—there came a ring to my bell, about the hour when a man gives his first yawn and glances at the clock. I sat up in my chair, and my wife laid her needle-work down in her lap and made a little face of disappointment.

“A patient!” said she. “You’ll have to go out.”

I groaned, for I was newly come back from a weary day.

We heard the door open, a few hurried words, and then quick steps upon the linoleum. Our own door flew open, and a lady, clad in some dark-coloured stuff, with a black veil, entered the room.

“You will excuse my calling so late,” she began, and then, suddenly losing her self-control, she ran forward, threw her arms about my wife’s neck, and sobbed upon her shoulder. “Oh, I’m in such trouble!” she cried; “I do so want a little help.”

“Why,” said my wife, pulling up her veil, “it is Kate Whitney. How you startled me, Kate! I had not an idea who you were when you came in.”

“I didn’t know what to do, so I came straight to you.” That was always the way. Folk who were in grief came to my wife like birds to a lighthouse.

“It was very sweet of you to come. Now, you must have some wine and water, and sit here comfortably and tell us all about it. Or should you rather that I sent James off to bed?”

“Oh, no, no! I want the doctor’s advice and help, too. It’s about Isa. He has not been home for two days. I am so frightened about him!”

It was not the first time that she had spoken to us of her husband’s trouble, to me as a doctor, to my wife as an old friend and school companion. We soothed and comforted her by such words as we could find. Did she know where her husband was? Was it possible that we could bring him back to her?

It seems that it was. She had the surest information that of late he had, when the fit was on him, made use of an opium den in the farthest east of the City. Hitherto his orgies had always been confined to one day, and he had come back, twitching and shattered, in the evening. But now the spell had been upon him eight-and-forty hours, and he lay there, doubtless among the dregs of the docks, breathing in the poison or sleeping off the effects. There he was to be found, she was sure of it, at the Bar of Gold, in Upper Swandam Lane. But what was she to do? How could she, a young and timid woman, make her way into such a place and pluck her husband out from among the ruffians who surrounded him?

It was shortly after five o’clock on a wet November evening when Miss Clara Bell was shown into our sitting-room at Baker Street. The rain beat steadily against the panes, and our visitor, though protected by a dark cloak, carried upon her hat and shoulders the unmistakable traces of the storm.

“I must catch the six-forty train from Euston,” she began, “but my return railway ticket has disappeared.”

Holmes, who had been stretched upon the sofa with his long fingers joined beneath his chin, sat upright.

“You are certain that you possessed it when you left home?”

“Entirely certain. I placed it in my purse after breakfast. At luncheon I opened the purse to pay a bill, and I believe I saw it then. Yet when I looked again, scarcely twenty minutes ago, it was gone.”

She emptied her purse upon the table. There were coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and several receipts, but no ticket. I examined the clasp and lining while Holmes watched Miss Bell rather than the objects.

“Where have you been since luncheon?” he asked.

“To a bookseller in the Strand, then to a tea-room, and finally here. I walked part of the way and took a cab for the rest.”

“You suspect theft?”

“I hardly know what to think.”

Holmes shook his head. “There has been no theft.”

He rose and glanced at the chair beside her. Upon it lay a folded newspaper, its outer pages darkened by rain. Holmes picked it up, weighed it in his hand, and turned it over.

“You bought this today?”

“Yes, outside the tea-room. I read it while waiting for my cab.”

“In the street?”

“No, indoors. I folded it before I left.”

Holmes opened the paper slightly, then smiled. The outer sheet was wet and cold, but the newspaper’s interior was perfectly dry.

“Your ticket is here,” said he.

Miss Bell stared as Holmes unfolded the pages. From between two inner sheets slipped the missing return ticket, which fluttered neatly onto the carpet.

I confess that the result appeared to me more magical than logical.

“You placed the ticket there while reading,” Holmes explained. “Perhaps you took it from your purse while searching for a coin, or perhaps you wished to keep your place in the newspaper. The exact impulse is immaterial. What matters is that the paper was folded before you went into the rain. Had the ticket been dropped upon it afterward, it would have rested among the damp outer leaves. Since the interior remained dry, anything accidentally enclosed before your departure would remain dry and concealed. Your recollection accounted for the purse; the rain accounted for the newspaper.”

Miss Bell recovered her property with such relief that she laughed aloud. There was still ample time for Euston, and I secured her a cab.

“A case without a criminal,” I remarked when I returned upstairs.

“Those are often the pleasantest, Watson,” said Holmes, resuming his place upon the sofa. “One may restore what is lost without adding to the number of the guilty.”

It was upon a wet evening in October, when the rain beat fitfully against the windows of our sitting-room in Baker Street, that Mrs Hudson ushered in a young lady whose agitation was scarcely concealed by her composed manner. She gave her name as Clara Bell, and from the drops upon her cloak and the damp curls at her temples it was plain that she had come to us through the storm.

“My return railway ticket is gone, Mr Holmes,” she cried. “My train departs from Euston at twenty minutes to seven—6:40 precisely—and I have searched everywhere.”

Holmes glanced at the clock. It wanted thirty-five minutes to the hour.

“You came directly here?”

“Yes. I had been taking tea with my aunt in Marylebone. I possessed the ticket when I arrived, for I placed it upon the hall table while removing my gloves. Before leaving, I picked it up with my newspaper—or so I believed.”

She laid upon our table a folded evening paper, its outer sheets darkened and limp with rain. Holmes did not touch it at once.

“Who was present in the house?”

“My aunt, her maid, and a young footman. But I cannot believe—”

“You are quite right,” said Holmes. “There has been no theft.”

Clara Bell stared at him, while I confess that his certainty astonished me.

“You carried a handbag?”

She handed it over. Holmes examined its compartments, then surveyed the gloves, purse, handkerchief, and small book which she had already placed before us. The ticket was not among them.

“You opened your newspaper during the journey here?” he asked.

“No. The rain was too heavy, and I held it over my muff.”

“Precisely.”

He lifted the paper delicately by one corner. The outer fold was thoroughly wet, and a little stream ran from it upon the polished wood. Holmes then opened it. The interior pages, sheltered by the folds, were perfectly dry.

“There is your answer,” said he.

With a long finger he separated two inner sheets. From between them fluttered the missing return ticket.

Miss Bell gave a little cry of relief. “But how could you know?”

“The outer paper has been exposed to the rain,” Holmes replied, “yet its interior is dry. Therefore it has remained folded since you left your aunt’s house. You told us that you lifted the ticket with the newspaper. Had the ticket fallen in the street, it would be wet; had you placed it in your bag, we should have found it there. Since no one stole it, the only remaining possibility was that it slipped between the dry inner pages when you gathered up the folded paper.”

Within five minutes our grateful visitor was in a cab bound for Euston. Holmes watched the streaming window in silence.

“You see, Watson,” he remarked at last, “men seek villains where a little rain and a folded newspaper contain the whole mystery.”

Among the minor problems which came under the notice of Sherlock Holmes, there were some which impressed themselves upon my memory more firmly than many an affair of violence and public consequence. Such was the curious incident of Miss Clara Bell’s return railway ticket, where a London downpour supplied my friend with the essential clue.

It was a little after five upon a bleak November evening. Rain drummed upon the windows of our Baker Street sitting-room, while the street lamps burned as pale and misty blurs in the gathering darkness. Holmes lay stretched upon the sofa, his long fingers joined beneath his chin, when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose anxious face contrasted sharply with her composed manner. Her cloak glistened with rain, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer pages limp and discoloured from the weather.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “My train leaves Euston at six-forty, Mr Holmes, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Holmes opened his eyes.

“When did you last see it?”

“This morning, in my purse. I looked into the purse again at luncheon, and I believe it was still there.”

At his request she emptied it upon the table. There were several coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and a little collection of receipts. I searched each compartment with some care, even examining the lining for a tear. Nothing rewarded me.

“Tell me your movements since luncheon,” said Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, and then came here in a cab after walking for a short distance.”

“Someone may have stolen it,” I suggested.

Our visitor started, but Holmes waved the notion aside.

“No theft has occurred, Watson.”

He rose and crossed to the chair upon which Miss Bell had laid her newspaper. The exposed surface was sodden, and drops had gathered along one crumpled edge.

“You bought this near the tea-room?” he asked.

“Yes. I read it while waiting for my cab, folded it indoors, and carried it beneath my arm.”

Holmes lifted the paper. With his delicate touch he parted the outer sheets and then the inner ones. The former were cold and saturated; the newspaper’s interior was dry. His lean face brightened with that swift, intent animation which I had learned to recognise as the herald of a solution.

“Your ticket is here.”

He opened the folded newspaper, and the missing return ticket fluttered from between the interior pages to the hearthrug.

Miss Bell uttered a cry of delight.

“You took it from your purse at the tea-room,” Holmes explained, “most likely when searching for money. In a moment of distraction you placed it within the paper, perhaps to mark your place, and folded the whole before stepping into the rain. Observe that the inner leaves remain perfectly dry. The ticket must therefore have been enclosed before the shower reached the paper. Had it slipped among the pages afterwards, it would have rested against damp newsprint.”

I secured a cab for Miss Bell, who departed in excellent time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

“No criminal, then,” said I, when I returned.

Holmes settled once more upon the sofa.

“None, Watson. Carelessness can construct a mystery without requiring a culprit.”

“Yes.”

Among the minor problems which came beneath the notice of Sherlock Holmes, there were several which, though devoid of crime, displayed his peculiar faculties as clearly as graver affairs. I recall in particular the adventure of Miss Clara Bell’s return railway ticket, for in that modest mystery the weather itself supplied the decisive clue.

It was a little after five on a bleak November evening. Rain beat sharply upon the windows of our Baker Street sitting-room, and the lamps beyond the glass shone as vague yellow stains in the gathering darkness. Holmes was stretched upon the sofa, his long fingers joined beneath his chin, while I sat beside the fire with a medical journal. Our landlady entered to announce a visitor.

The young lady who followed her was pale with anxiety. Drops sparkled upon her dark cloak, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer surface blackened with wet.

“My name is Clara Bell,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Holmes glanced towards the clock.

“You have searched your purse?”

“Again and again.”

She emptied it upon the table. There were some coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and three receipts. I examined the lining with the thoroughness of my profession, but found neither tear nor hidden pocket.

“When did you last see the ticket?” asked Holmes.

“This morning, after breakfast. I believe it was still there at luncheon.”

“And since then?”

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, took tea, walked a short distance, and came here in a cab. I discovered the loss less than twenty minutes ago.”

“Then someone may have taken it,” I suggested.

Miss Bell looked alarmed, but Holmes shook his head.

“No theft has occurred, Watson. We have no culprit to pursue.”

He rose and crossed to the chair upon which the newspaper now rested. Water had collected beneath it in a little shining curve. Holmes lifted the folded sheets, observed their edges, and opened them gently. The exterior was sodden from the rain, yet the newspaper’s interior was dry.

His face brightened with that sudden, intent animation which so often told me that the matter was finished while I remained at its beginning.

“Your ticket lies within these pages, Miss Bell.”

He unfolded the newspaper over the hearthrug. From between two inner leaves the missing return railway ticket fluttered to the floor.

Our visitor gave a cry of delight. “But how could you know?”

“You read the paper while taking tea,” said Holmes. “At some moment you removed the ticket with your money and placed it between the open leaves, perhaps to mark an item. You afterwards folded the newspaper and carried it beneath your arm into the rain. See: the outer sheets are wet, but those inside remain perfectly dry. Therefore anything enclosed among the dry leaves must have been placed there before you went out into the storm.”

Within minutes I had found Miss Bell a cab, and she departed in good time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

When I returned upstairs, Holmes had resumed his place upon the sofa.

“A mystery without a villain,” said I.

“Precisely, Watson. Human absent-mindedness is quite capable of providing one.”

The little adventure of Clara Bell’s return railway ticket is a case in point. It involved no crime, no violence, and, as Holmes was quick to declare, no culprit; yet it afforded a neat example of that exact observation which so often seemed miraculous to those who witnessed it.

It was a few minutes past five upon a bleak November evening. The rain beat sharply against our windows in Baker Street, while the yellow lamps below shone dimly through the streaming panes. Holmes was stretched upon the sofa, his long fingers joined beneath his chin, when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose troubled face contrasted strangely with her composed manner.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Her cloak was dark with rain, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer surface limp and mottled with wet. At Holmes’s request she emptied her purse upon the table. There were several coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and a collection of small receipts. I searched each division with medical thoroughness, but the ticket was not there.

“You had it this morning?” Holmes asked.

“I saw it after breakfast. I believe it was still in my purse at luncheon.”

“And since then?”

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand and afterwards took tea. I bought the newspaper outside the tea-room, read it while waiting for a cab, and folded it before I stepped into the rain. I discovered my loss shortly before coming here.”

“Then someone may have taken it,” I suggested.

Miss Bell turned pale, but Holmes shook his head.

“There has been no theft, Watson.”

He rose and crossed to the chair upon which she had placed the newspaper. A crescent of moisture had formed beneath it. Holmes lifted the folded sheets, examined their edges, and then gently separated them. The outer pages were soaked and cold, while the newspaper’s interior was dry.

His lean face sharpened in an instant.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He opened the paper upon the table. From between two inner pages the missing return ticket fluttered down before us.

“I cannot imagine how it came there!” she exclaimed.

“The explanation is commonplace,” said Holmes. “At the tea-room you opened your purse, perhaps to pay for some refreshment, and drew out the ticket with your coins. While reading, you slipped it between the pages, whether as a marker or through simple distraction. You folded the newspaper before leaving shelter. “My dear Watson,” said he, closing his eyes, “human absent-mindedness has supplied puzzles enough to rival human wickedness.”

Among the minor problems which came under the notice of Sherlock Holmes, I have found more than one which returns to my memory with a freshness denied to graver affairs. There was no crime, no villain, and no injured party in the adventure of Clara Bell; yet it displayed so neatly my friend’s peculiar faculty for extracting certainty from a commonplace detail that I cannot forbear to record it.

It was nearing six upon a wet November evening. Rain hissed against the panes of our Baker Street sitting-room, while the street lamps shone through the watery gloom like blurred yellow stars. Holmes lay upon the sofa with his long fingers joined beneath his chin, and I had drawn close to the fire, when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose dripping cloak bore witness to the violence of the weather.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I have lost my return railway ticket.”

She spoke with composure, but her quick breath and anxious eyes betrayed her. Beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, darkened upon its outer surface with rain.

“You had the ticket this morning?” asked Holmes.

“I saw it in my purse after breakfast. At luncheon I opened the purse again, and I believe it was still there.”

At his request she emptied the little receptacle upon our table. Coins, keys, receipts, and a lace handkerchief lay before us. I searched each division and passed a finger beneath the lining. Nothing rewarded me.

“Since luncheon?”

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, then took tea. I bought this newspaper outside the tea-room, read it while waiting for a cab, and folded it before I came away. I discovered the loss shortly before reaching Baker Street.”

“Then someone may have taken it,” I suggested.

Miss Bell turned pale.

“No,” said Holmes. “No theft has occurred.”

He rose with that sudden energy which so often followed his deepest languor, crossed to our visitor, and took the newspaper from her. Water glistened upon the exposed sheets, and a wet stain marked the chair where it had rested. Holmes opened the fold. The newspaper’s interior was dry.

A moment later his thin face brightened.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He unfolded the paper upon the table, and from between two inner pages the missing return ticket fluttered down. Our client uttered a cry of relief.

“You withdrew it at the tea-room,” Holmes explained, “most likely when taking out money. In a moment of abstraction you placed it between the open leaves. Then you folded the newspaper and went into the rain. Observe: the outside is soaked, while the enclosed pages remain perfectly dry. I secured a cab, and Clara Bell departed in ample time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

They involved neither violence nor scandal, yet each offered some small point upon which his singular faculty could fasten. Such was the affair of Clara Bell and the missing railway ticket.

It was nearing six upon a wet November evening. The rain drummed steadily against our Baker Street windows, while the yellow lamps shone through the streaming panes as blurred circles of fire. Holmes lay upon the sofa, his long fingers joined beneath his chin, when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose frightened expression contrasted strangely with her composed manner.

“My name is Clara Bell,” she began. “My train leaves Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Her cloak glittered with rain. Beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, darkened and limp upon its exposed surface.

Holmes requested her to sit down and tell us when she had last seen the ticket.

“It was in my purse this morning. I believe I noticed it again when I paid for luncheon.”

At his invitation she emptied the purse upon our table. There were coins, two keys, several receipts, and a handkerchief edged with lace. I examined the compartments with the care of a surgeon probing a wound, but the missing ticket was not there.

“Someone may have taken the ticket,” I suggested.

Clara Bell turned pale.

“No,” said Holmes quietly. “No theft has occurred.”

He rose and crossed to the chair upon which she had placed the newspaper. A small pool had formed beneath it. The outer leaves were sodden, and the print had run in several places; but when Holmes opened the fold and touched the sheets within, I saw that the newspaper’s interior was dry.

His whole aspect changed. The languor vanished, and his grey eyes shone with that concentrated brightness which I had learned to recognise as the herald of a conclusion.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He unfolded the newspaper upon the table. From between two inner pages the return railway ticket slipped forth and fluttered to the rug.

Our client uttered a cry of delight.

“The matter is quite plain,” Holmes explained. “While at tea you took the ticket from your purse, most likely with some loose money, and placed it among the open pages without conscious thought. You folded the paper before stepping into the rain. Observe that the wet has reached only the outside. I secured a cab for Clara Bell, who departed in excellent time to catch the six-forty from Euston.

“A mystery without a criminal,” said I.

Among the lesser problems which came before my friend, there are some that remain more vividly in my memory than affairs attended by danger or public scandal. Such was the singular little incident of Miss Clara Bell’s railway ticket, in which a shower of rain supplied the one piece of evidence required.

It was shortly after five upon a November evening that our landlady admitted a young lady to the sitting-room in Baker Street. Rain rattled against the windows, and the lamps glimmered faintly through the watery dusk. Our visitor’s dark cloak shone with moisture, while a folded newspaper, tucked beneath her arm, was stained by the weather.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “I must leave Euston by the train at six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

Holmes, who had lain silent upon the sofa, raised himself upon one elbow.

“Where did Miss Bell last see it?”

“In my purse after breakfast. I opened the purse again at luncheon, and I am almost certain it was there.”

She poured its contents upon the table: a few coins, two small keys, some receipts, and a lace handkerchief. I examined every compartment, even running my finger beneath the lining, but without success.

“Since luncheon?” Holmes asked.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea, and came on by cab after walking some distance. I noticed the loss not twenty minutes ago.”

“Could anyone have taken it?”

The anxiety in her face deepened at this disquieting possibility, but Holmes dismissed it with a languid movement of his hand.

“No theft has occurred.”

He had risen now, and his attention rested upon the newspaper beside her. Its exposed surface was sodden and dark, and a little crescent of water had gathered upon the chair beneath it.

“This was purchased at the tea-room?”

“Just outside it. I read it indoors while awaiting my cab, folded it there, and carried it under my arm.”

Holmes lifted the paper and separated two of its leaves. The outer sheets were chilled and wet; the newspaper’s interior was dry. At once his keen face took on that alert expression which announced the end of a problem.

“The ticket is inside,” said he.

Miss Bell gave a cry of astonishment. Holmes unfolded the newspaper with deliberate care, and from between its inner pages the missing return ticket slid to the carpet.

“The sequence is plain,” he continued. “At the tea-room you removed the ticket from your purse—perhaps with some coins—and slipped it between the pages, either as a marker or from momentary abstraction. You then folded the paper before going out. The rain has penetrated the exterior only. Had the ticket become entangled with the newspaper later, it must have lain among the damp leaves. A dry interior pointed to something enclosed before the paper met the storm.”

Miss Bell’s relief was charming to behold. I found her a cab, and she departed with ample time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

“So there is no villain after all,” I remarked upon returning.

Holmes resumed his place upon the sofa.

“My dear Watson, an error may furnish a mystery quite adequately. It has, moreover, the rare merit of requiring no culprit.”

Among the minor adventures which I have preserved in my notebooks, there are several that possess, in my recollection, a freshness denied to graver affairs. One such incident concerned Miss Clara Bell, a railway journey, and a circumstance so trifling that I had observed it without understanding it.

It was a little after five on a wet November evening. The rain drummed upon the panes of our Baker Street sitting-room, while the yellow lamps beyond them burned as dimly as candles seen through smoked glass. Holmes lay upon the sofa with his long fingers joined beneath his chin when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose anxious expression contrasted strangely with her composed manner.

“My name is Clara Bell,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Her cloak glistened with rain. Beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer sheets darkened and limp from the weather.

Holmes glanced at the clock.

“You last saw the ticket when?”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe it was still there at luncheon.”

At his request she emptied the purse upon our table. There were several coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and a confusion of receipts. I searched every pocket and seam with the thoroughness of a medical examination, but the ticket was not there.

“Tell us your movements since luncheon,” said Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, bought that newspaper, and read it while waiting for a cab. I had to walk some distance before finding one. It was then that the rain began.”

“Someone may have taken the ticket,” I suggested.

Miss Bell turned pale, but Holmes shook his head.

“No theft has occurred, Watson.”

He rose and extended his hand for the newspaper. Water had gathered along its creases, and a dark patch marked the chair where it had rested. Holmes opened it gently. The outer leaves clung together with moisture; yet, as he parted the close-folded sheets, I saw that the newspaper’s interior was dry.

His grey eyes brightened.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He opened the paper completely, and the missing return ticket fluttered from between two inner pages to the hearthrug.

Our visitor stared at it in silence before relief overcame her astonishment.

“You took it from your purse at the tea-room,” Holmes explained, “probably when searching for coins. In your abstraction you placed it inside the newspaper, then folded the paper before stepping into the rain. The outside became saturated, but the enclosed pages remained protected. Since the ticket lay among those dry leaves, it must have been inserted before the shower reached you.”

I secured a cab for Miss Bell, who left us with sufficient time to catch the six-forty from Euston.

When I returned, Holmes had resumed his place upon the sofa.

“A mystery without a criminal,” said I.

“Precisely, Watson. Carelessness supplies enigmas more frequently than wickedness, though it receives much less attention.”

To Sherlock Holmes she is always _the_ woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

---

“My dear fellow,” said Sherlock Holmes as we sat on either side of the fire in his lodgings at Baker Street, “life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence. If we could fly out of that window hand in hand, hover over this great city, gently remove the roofs, and peep in at the queer things which are going on, the strange coincidences, the plannings, the cross-purposes, the wonderful chains of events, working through generations, and leading to the most _outré_ results, it would make all fiction with its conventionalities and foreseen conclusions most stale and unprofitable.”

“And yet I am not convinced of it,” I answered. “The cases which come to light in the papers are, as a rule, bald enough, and vulgar enough. We have in our police reports realism pushed to its extreme limits, and yet the result is, it must be confessed, neither fascinating nor artistic.”

“A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect,” remarked Holmes. “This is wanting in the police report, where more stress is laid, perhaps, upon the platitudes of the magistrate than upon the details, which to an observer contain the vital essence of the whole matter. Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.”

I smiled and shook my head. “I can quite understand your thinking so,” I said. “Of course, in your position of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled, throughout three continents, you are brought in contact with all that is strange and bizarre. But here”—I picked up the morning paper from the ground—“let us put it to a practical test. Here is the first heading upon which I come. ‘A husband’s cruelty to his wife.’ There is half a column of print, but I know without reading it that it is all perfectly familiar to me. There is, of course, the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, the sympathetic sister or landlady. The crudest of writers could invent nothing more crude.”

“Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument,” said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. “This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.”

He held out his snuffbox of old gold, with a great amethyst in the centre of the lid. Its splendour was in such contrast to his homely ways and simple life that I could not help commenting upon it.

---

When I glance over my notes and records of the Sherlock Holmes cases between the years ’82 and ’90, I am faced by so many which present strange and interesting features that it is no easy matter to know which to choose and which to leave. Some, however, have already gained publicity through the papers, and others have not offered a field for those peculiar qualities which my friend possessed in so high a degree, and which it is the object of these papers to illustrate. Some, too, have baffled his analytical skill, and would be, as narratives, beginnings without an ending, while others have been but partially cleared up, and have their explanations founded rather upon conjecture and surmise than on that absolute logical proof which was so dear to him. There is, however, one of these last which was so remarkable in its details and so startling in its results that I am tempted to give some account of it in spite of the fact that there are points in connection with it which never have been, and probably never will be, entirely cleared up.

The year ’87 furnished us with a long series of cases of greater or less interest, of which I retain the records. Among my headings under this one twelve months I find an account of the adventure of the Paradol Chamber, of the Amateur Mendicant Society, who held a luxurious club in the lower vault of a furniture warehouse, of the facts connected with the loss of the British barque _Sophy Anderson_, of the singular adventures of the Grice Patersons in the island of Uffa, and finally of the Camberwell poisoning case. In the latter, as may be remembered, Sherlock Holmes was able, by winding up the dead man’s watch, to prove that it had been wound up two hours before, and that therefore the deceased had gone to bed within that time—a deduction which was of the greatest importance in clearing up the case. All these I may sketch out at some future date, but none of them present such singular features as the strange train of circumstances which I have now taken up my pen to describe.

It was in the latter days of September, and the equinoctial gales had set in with exceptional violence. All day the wind had screamed and the rain had beaten against the windows, so that even here in the heart of great, hand-made London we were forced to raise our minds for the instant from the routine of life and to recognise the presence of those great elemental forces which shriek at mankind through the bars of his civilisation, like untamed beasts in a cage. As evening drew in, the storm grew higher and louder, and the wind cried and sobbed like a child in the chimney. Sherlock Holmes sat moodily at one side of the fireplace cross-indexing his records of crime, while I at the other was deep in one of Clark Russell’s fine sea-stories until the howl of the gale from without seemed to blend with the text, and the splash of the rain to lengthen out into the long swash of the sea waves. My wife was on a visit to her mother’s, and for a few days I was a dweller once more in my old quarters at Baker Street.

Among the smaller problems which came beneath my notice during my association with Sherlock Holmes, there were several which impressed me more deeply than cases involving violence and scandal. One such affair concerned Miss Clara Bell and a missing railway ticket, though the whole mystery occupied scarcely twenty minutes.

It was a little after five on a bleak November evening. Rain drummed fitfully upon the windows of our Baker Street rooms, while the yellow lamps below shone as blurred islands in the streaming roadway. I was drawing my chair nearer to the fire when Mrs Hudson ushered in a young lady whose agitated face contrasted sharply with her composed manner. Her cloak was wet at the shoulders, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, darkened by the rain.

“I am Clara Bell,” she began. “My train leaves Euston at six-forty, Mr Holmes, and I have lost my return railway ticket.”

Holmes, who had been stretched upon the sofa with closed eyes, looked up.

“When did you last see it?”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe that it was still there at luncheon.”

At his request she emptied the purse upon our table. There were some coins, two keys, several receipts, and a small lace handkerchief. I inspected the compartments and even examined the lining, but the ticket was certainly absent.

“You have been where since luncheon?” Holmes asked.

“At a bookseller’s in the Strand, and afterwards at a tea-room. I walked for some distance before taking a cab here.”

“And you fear that someone has stolen it?”

“I cannot otherwise explain its disappearance.”

“No theft has occurred,” said Holmes quietly.

Miss Bell stared at him, but his gaze had already passed from her face to the newspaper upon the chair. Its outer fold was soaked, and drops had gathered along its lower edge.

“You read that at the tea-room?”

“Yes. I bought it outside, read it while waiting for my cab, folded it indoors, and carried it beneath my arm.”

Holmes took up the paper. He opened the first sheet, then another. The exterior was clammy and rain-stained, but the newspaper’s interior was dry. His long, nervous fingers paused, and a gleam of satisfaction came into his eyes.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He unfolded the newspaper completely. From between two inner leaves the missing return ticket fluttered down upon the hearth-rug.

I confess that the result astonished me scarcely less than it delighted our visitor.

“You removed it with your money at the tea-room,” Holmes explained, “and slipped it unconsciously into the open paper. Then you folded the newspaper before stepping into the rain. Observe that the inner leaves remain perfectly dry. Anything introduced after your walk must have touched a wet surface. Since the ticket was placed among dry pages, it entered before the outer sheets encountered the storm.”

Miss Bell departed in a cab with sufficient time to reach Euston for the six-forty. When I returned upstairs, Holmes had resumed his former position.

“There was no criminal, then,” said I.

“My dear Watson,” he replied, “carelessness can construct a mystery without requiring a culprit.”

Beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its exposed sheets stained almost black by the downpour.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at 6:40, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Holmes opened his eyes.

“When did you last see it?”

“This morning, in my purse. I looked into the purse again at luncheon, and believe it was still there.”

At his request she emptied it upon the table. There were coins, two keys, several receipts, and a lace handkerchief. I examined each compartment with considerable care, even probing beneath the silk lining, but the ticket was not there.

“Tell me your movements since luncheon,” said Holmes.

“Then someone may have stolen it,” I suggested.

Miss Bell turned pale, but Holmes waved the notion aside.

“No theft has occurred, Watson. There is no culprit.”

He rose and crossed to the chair upon which she had placed her newspaper. Water had collected beneath it in a small crescent. Holmes lifted the folded bundle, examined its edges, and gently parted the leaves. The outer pages were sodden; the newspaper’s interior was dry.

His whole manner changed. The languor vanished, and his grey eyes became keen with that cold brightness which I had learned to associate with a solution.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He opened the paper fully. From between two inner sheets the missing return ticket fluttered to the carpet.

Our visitor stared at him in astonishment.

You folded the paper before stepping into the rain. Observe the consequence: moisture has reached the exterior, yet within all remains perfectly dry. One such affair concerned Miss Clara Bell and a missing railway ticket; and though it occupied scarcely half an hour, it displayed with singular neatness my friend’s habit of extracting significance from the most commonplace detail.

It was a little after five on a wet November evening. The rain, which had fallen without interruption since noon, hissed against the panes of our Baker Street sitting-room, while the street lamps showed as blurred yellow stains in the gathering darkness. I was drawing nearer to the fire when our landlady ushered in a young woman whose anxious face contrasted sharply with her composed manner.

“My name is Clara Bell,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Her cloak was glistening with rain, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer pages limp and darkened. Holmes, stretched upon the sofa, opened his eyes.

“When did you last see the ticket?”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe that I saw it again at luncheon, though I cannot swear to it.”

She emptied the purse upon our table. There were coins, two keys, a handkerchief, and several receipts. I searched each pocket and examined the lining with some care.

Nothing.

“Your movements since luncheon?” asked Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, then took tea, and afterwards walked until I found a cab. I discovered the loss upon arriving here.”

“Then someone may have stolen it,” said I.

Miss Bell turned pale, but Holmes gave a brief, impatient shake of the head.

“No theft has occurred, Watson.”

He had fixed his gaze upon the newspaper. Taking it from our visitor, he touched the sodden outer fold and then gently parted the sheets near the centre. The newspaper’s interior was dry.

Holmes smiled.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He opened the paper fully, and from between two inner pages the missing return ticket fluttered down upon the hearthrug. Our client stared at it in delighted amazement.

“You bought the newspaper before taking tea,” Holmes continued. “While indoors you removed something from your purse—probably money—and drew out the ticket with it. Being occupied with the paper, you placed the ticket between its pages and subsequently folded them around it. Then you stepped into the rain. Observe that the outer sheets are saturated, yet those within remain perfectly dry. The ticket, therefore, was enclosed before the newspaper became wet. Its hiding-place followed inevitably.”

Miss Bell’s relief left no room for embarrassment. I secured a cab for her, and she departed in good time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

“A mystery without a criminal,” I remarked.

“Precisely, Watson. Carelessness is a prolific conspirator, but fortunately it requires no culprit.”

Among the minor incidents preserved in my notebooks, there are several which, though lacking every element of crime, display my friend’s peculiar faculties more clearly than many a celebrated investigation. The affair of Clara Bell’s return railway ticket was one of these. It occupied scarcely twenty minutes, yet I recall it whenever rain beats upon the windows of Baker Street.

It was a little after five on a bleak November evening. The lamps had already been lit, and their blurred radiance floated upon the streaming panes, while Holmes, stretched upon the sofa, regarded the ceiling with that profound vacancy which in him was often the mask of intense attention. Our landlady entered, followed closely by a young woman in a dark travelling cloak.

She was pale with agitation. Drops sparkled upon her shoulders, and beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper whose outer leaves were sodden.

“I am Clara Bell,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

Holmes sat up.

“When did you last see it?”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe it was still there at luncheon.”

At his request she emptied the purse upon our table. There were coins, receipts, two keys, and a handkerchief of fine lace. I searched each pocket and pressed the lining between my fingers, but discovered nothing.

“Tell us your movements since luncheon,” said Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, took tea, and waited indoors for a cab. It set me down some distance away, so I walked here through the rain. I found the ticket gone just before I reached your door.”

“Then someone has stolen it!” I exclaimed.

Clara Bell turned sharply, but Holmes merely shook his head.

“No theft has occurred, Watson.”

His long fingers had closed upon the newspaper. He examined the darkened outer fold, upon which the rain had left an irregular stain. Then he opened it at the centre and touched the inner pages.

“Quite dry,” said he.

The change in his manner was instantaneous. His listlessness vanished, and his eyes shone with the keen satisfaction of a man who has reached firm ground after wandering through mist.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He spread the newspaper upon the table. From between two interior sheets there slipped a small rectangle of pasteboard. Clara Bell caught it up with a cry, and for an instant could only stare from the ticket to Holmes.

“You bought the paper before taking tea,” he explained. “While indoors you removed the ticket from your purse, most likely when paying for some refreshment. In your distraction you placed it between the open pages, then folded the newspaper and carried it beneath your arm. Observe the essential point: the exterior is wet, but the newspaper’s interior is dry. Therefore anything enclosed among those inner leaves before you stepped into the rain would remain protected. The missing ticket had not travelled far.”

I secured a cab for our grateful visitor, and she left Baker Street with sufficient time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

When I returned, Holmes had resumed his place upon the sofa.

“A case without a villain,” said I.

“The commonest sort, Watson,” he replied. “Human inattention contrives mysteries enough without requiring a culprit.”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe that it was still there when I paid for luncheon.”

“Tell me what followed luncheon,” said Holmes.

Among the minor adventures of Sherlock Holmes there are several which, though they involved neither violence nor scandal, remain fixed in my memory with a peculiar distinctness. One such affair concerned Miss Clara Bell, a return railway ticket, and a sheet of wet newspaper; yet it displayed, within its modest compass, the exact and luminous reasoning which was so characteristic of my friend.

It was upon a rainy November evening that Mrs Hudson ushered a young lady into our sitting-room in Baker Street. The lamps had already been lit, though the clock showed only a little after five, and their yellow radiance scarcely penetrated the streaming windows. Our visitor’s cloak was dark with rain. Beneath one arm she carried a folded newspaper, whose outer pages hung limp and sodden.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she, with considerable agitation. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and I cannot find my return railway ticket.”

Holmes, who had been stretched upon the sofa with his long fingers joined beneath his chin, opened his eyes.

“When did you last see it?”

“This morning, in my purse. I believe it was still there when I paid for luncheon.”

At his request she emptied the little leather purse upon the table. There were coins, two keys, several receipts, and a lace handkerchief. I searched each compartment with medical thoroughness, even examining the lining, but the ticket was certainly not there.

“Tell me your movements since luncheon,” said Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, and waited there for a cab. I walked some distance before finding one, and it was then that the rain began.”

“Could it have been stolen?” I asked.

Miss Bell turned pale, but Holmes gave a slight impatient shrug.

“No theft has occurred, Watson. Pray observe before you alarm our client.”

He had risen and was now bending over the newspaper which she had placed upon a chair. The exposed sheets were blackened with moisture, and drops had collected beneath one corner. Holmes picked it up, turned it once in his hands, and gently parted the fold.

The newspaper’s interior was dry.

I saw the quick brightness enter his grey eyes. It was the change which I had learned to recognise as surely as a mariner knows the first gleam of a beacon.

“Your ticket is here, Miss Bell.”

He opened the newspaper upon the table. From between two inner pages the missing return ticket fluttered down.

Our visitor stared at it in speechless relief.

“The matter is quite simple,” Holmes continued. “While you were taking tea, you removed the ticket with some coins and placed it inside the paper, perhaps to mark your place, perhaps through mere abstraction. You folded the newspaper before you stepped into the rain. Its outer leaves are saturated, while those within remain untouched. The ticket, therefore, must have been enclosed before the shower reached you.”

Miss Bell departed in a cab with ample time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

Among the lesser problems which came before my friend, there are some that remain more vividly in my memory than affairs attended by danger or public scandal. Such was the singular little incident of Miss Clara Bell’s railway ticket, in which a shower of rain supplied the one piece of evidence required.

It was shortly after five upon a November evening that our landlady admitted a young lady to the sitting-room in Baker Street. Rain rattled against the windows, and the lamps glimmered faintly through the watery dusk. Our visitor’s dark cloak shone with moisture, while a folded newspaper, tucked beneath her arm, was stained by the weather.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “I must leave Euston by the train at six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

Holmes, who had lain silent upon the sofa, raised himself upon one elbow.

“Where did Miss Bell last see it?”

“In my purse after breakfast. I opened the purse again at luncheon, and I am almost certain it was there.”

She poured its contents upon the table: a few coins, two small keys, some receipts, and a lace handkerchief. I examined every compartment, even running my finger beneath the lining, but without success.

“Since luncheon?” Holmes asked.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea, and came on by cab after walking some distance. I noticed the loss not twenty minutes ago.”

“Could anyone have taken it?”

The anxiety in her face deepened at this disquieting possibility, but Holmes dismissed it with a languid movement of his hand.

“No theft has occurred.”

He had risen now, and his attention rested upon the newspaper beside her. Its exposed surface was sodden and dark, and a little crescent of water had gathered upon the chair beneath it.

“This was purchased at the tea-room?”

“Just outside it. I read it indoors while awaiting my cab, folded it there, and carried it under my arm.”

Holmes lifted the paper and separated two of its leaves. The outer sheets were chilled and wet; the newspaper’s interior was dry. At once his keen face took on that alert expression which announced the end of a problem.

“The ticket is inside,” said he.

Miss Bell gave a cry of astonishment. Holmes unfolded the newspaper with deliberate care, and from between its inner pages the missing return ticket slid to the carpet.

“The sequence is plain,” he continued. “At the tea-room you removed the ticket from your purse—perhaps with some coins—and slipped it between the pages, either as a marker or from momentary abstraction. You then folded the paper before going out. The rain has penetrated the exterior only. Had the ticket become entangled with the newspaper later, it must have lain among the damp leaves. A dry interior pointed to something enclosed before the paper met the storm.”

Miss Bell’s relief was charming to behold. I found her a cab, and she departed with ample time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

“So there is no villain after all,” I remarked upon returning.

Holmes resumed his place upon the sofa.

“My dear Watson, an error may furnish a mystery quite adequately. It has, moreover, the rare merit of requiring no culprit.”

To Sherlock Holmes she is always _the_ woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

---

“My dear fellow,” said Sherlock Holmes as we sat on either side of the fire in his lodgings at Baker Street, “life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence. If we could fly out of that window hand in hand, hover over this great city, gently remove the roofs, and peep in at the queer things which are going on, the strange coincidences, the plannings, the cross-purposes, the wonderful chains of events, working through generations, and leading to the most _outré_ results, it would make all fiction with its conventionalities and foreseen conclusions most stale and unprofitable.”

“And yet I am not convinced of it,” I answered. “The cases which come to light in the papers are, as a rule, bald enough, and vulgar enough. We have in our police reports realism pushed to its extreme limits, and yet the result is, it must be confessed, neither fascinating nor artistic.”

“A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect,” remarked Holmes. “This is wanting in the police report, where more stress is laid, perhaps, upon the platitudes of the magistrate than upon the details, which to an observer contain the vital essence of the whole matter. Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.”

I smiled and shook my head. “I can quite understand your thinking so,” I said. “Of course, in your position of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled, throughout three continents, you are brought in contact with all that is strange and bizarre. But here”—I picked up the morning paper from the ground—“let us put it to a practical test. Here is the first heading upon which I come. ‘A husband’s cruelty to his wife.’ There is half a column of print, but I know without reading it that it is all perfectly familiar to me. There is, of course, the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, the sympathetic sister or landlady. The crudest of writers could invent nothing more crude.”

“Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument,” said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. “This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it.
