Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.”

He held out his snuffbox of old gold, with a great amethyst in the centre of the lid. Its splendour was in such contrast to his homely ways and simple life that I could not help commenting upon it.

---

When I glance over my notes and records of the Sherlock Holmes cases between the years ’82 and ’90, I am faced by so many which present strange and interesting features that it is no easy matter to know which to choose and which to leave. Some, however, have already gained publicity through the papers, and others have not offered a field for those peculiar qualities which my friend possessed in so high a degree, and which it is the object of these papers to illustrate. Some, too, have baffled his analytical skill, and would be, as narratives, beginnings without an ending, while others have been but partially cleared up, and have their explanations founded rather upon conjecture and surmise than on that absolute logical proof which was so dear to him. There is, however, one of these last which was so remarkable in its details and so startling in its results that I am tempted to give some account of it in spite of the fact that there are points in connection with it which never have been, and probably never will be, entirely cleared up.

The year ’87 furnished us with a long series of cases of greater or less interest, of which I retain the records. Among my headings under this one twelve months I find an account of the adventure of the Paradol Chamber, of the Amateur Mendicant Society, who held a luxurious club in the lower vault of a furniture warehouse, of the facts connected with the loss of the British barque _Sophy Anderson_, of the singular adventures of the Grice Patersons in the island of Uffa, and finally of the Camberwell poisoning case. In the latter, as may be remembered, Sherlock Holmes was able, by winding up the dead man’s watch, to prove that it had been wound up two hours before, and that therefore the deceased had gone to bed within that time—a deduction which was of the greatest importance in clearing up the case. All these I may sketch out at some future date, but none of them present such singular features as the strange train of circumstances which I have now taken up my pen to describe.

It was in the latter days of September, and the equinoctial gales had set in with exceptional violence. All day the wind had screamed and the rain had beaten against the windows, so that even here in the heart of great, hand-made London we were forced to raise our minds for the instant from the routine of life and to recognise the presence of those great elemental forces which shriek at mankind through the bars of his civilisation, like untamed beasts in a cage. As evening drew in, the storm grew higher and louder, and the wind cried and sobbed like a child in the chimney. Sherlock Holmes sat moodily at one side of the fireplace cross-indexing his records of crime, while I at the other was deep in one of Clark Russell’s fine sea-stories until the howl of the gale from without seemed to blend with the text, and the splash of the rain to lengthen out into the long swash of the sea waves. My wife was on a visit to her mother’s, and for a few days I was a dweller once more in my old quarters at Baker Street.

Among the lesser puzzles brought before Sherlock Holmes, there is one which I have often recalled, for it showed how a fact may lie in full view and yet escape every eye save his. No crime shadowed the affair. There was no culprit to expose, nor had any theft occurred. The matter concerned only Miss Clara Bell and a missing return railway ticket.

It was nearing five o’clock upon a dismal November afternoon. Rain rattled against the panes of our Baker Street room, and the lamps below glimmered through the murk like yellow stars seen under water. Holmes was stretched upon the sofa, silent and languid, while I tended the fire. Our landlady entered with a young lady whose pale face and hurried breath proclaimed her distress.

“My name is Clara Bell,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at 6:40, and I have lost my return railway ticket.”

Her cloak was wet at the shoulders. Beneath her arm she held a folded newspaper, its outer sheets darkened and softened by the rain.

Holmes rose at once.

“Where did you last see it?”

“In my purse this morning. I think I saw it again at luncheon.”

She poured the contents of the purse upon our table: coins, keys, two receipts, a pencil, and a square of lace. I examined every article, then the purse itself, with all the care of which I was capable. Holmes merely watched.

“Your movements since luncheon?” he asked.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, and walked for some distance before finding a cab. I noticed the loss twenty minutes ago. Could a thief have taken it?”

“There has been no theft,” said Holmes.

His quiet certainty amazed me. He had touched neither her purse nor her cloak. Instead, he pointed to the newspaper.

“You bought that near the tea room?”

“Yes. I read it over tea, folded it before going out, and kept it under my arm.”

Holmes lifted it from the chair. Drops stood upon the exposed fold, and a small crescent of water marked the upholstery. He opened the damp outer pages, then parted the leaves nearer the centre.

“The newspaper’s interior is dry,” I remarked.

“Precisely, Watson.”

He turned the paper downward and gave it one brisk shake. The missing ticket slipped from between the folded sheets and fell upon the hearthrug.

Miss Bell uttered a cry of relief.

“You took it from your purse at the tea table,” Holmes explained, “perhaps while reaching for a coin. You laid it upon the open paper and forgot it. The paper was then folded before you stepped into the rain. Its wet surface and dry interior prove that whatever lies among those inner leaves was enclosed before the storm touched them.”

I found Miss Bell a cab, and she reached Euston in good time for the 6:40.

“So ends a mystery without a villain,” said I on my return.

Holmes sank once more upon the sofa. “My dear Watson, villains are plentiful. A dry sheet in a wet newspaper is far more instructive.”

Among the lesser problems brought to Sherlock Holmes, there is one which I have often recalled, for it showed how a plain fact may escape the eye until reason gives it a voice. The matter involved no crime, nor had any person acted with guile. It concerned only Miss Clara Bell and a missing return railway ticket.

Rain had fallen since noon, and by five o’clock Baker Street lay behind a grey curtain. The drops rattled on the panes, the fire burned low, and Holmes had stretched his spare form upon the sofa with the air of a man to whom London had offered nothing worthy of notice.

Our door opened, and a young lady entered in some distress. Her cloak shone with wet, and beneath her arm she carried a folded newspaper, sodden at the edges.

“I am Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at six forty. I have lost my return ticket.”

Holmes raised his eyes.

“You had it earlier?”

“It was in my purse this morning, and I am nearly certain that I saw it at luncheon.”

At his request she placed the contents of her purse upon the table. I examined the coins, two small keys, a handkerchief, and several receipts. I even ran my finger along the torn silk lining. The ticket was not there.

“Your movements since luncheon?” asked Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, then to a tea room. I bought this newspaper outside, read it over my tea, and folded it before stepping into the rain. Afterwards I took a cab here.”

“Could someone have stolen the ticket?”

“No one has stolen it,” said Holmes.

His certainty amazed me, for he had scarcely stirred. Now he rose, took the newspaper from Miss Bell, and held it near the lamp. The exposed sheets were dark with rain, and a thin stream crept from one corner to the floor. He opened the fold. The outer pages dragged against one another, but the newspaper’s interior was dry.

That was enough.

“Your ticket lies inside these sheets,” said he.

A brisk shake followed, and the missing return ticket slipped from between two inner pages and fell beside the hearth. Miss Bell gave a cry of relief.

“You drew it from your purse at the tea room,” Holmes continued, “perhaps while seeking a coin, and laid it upon the open paper. Your attention wandered; you folded the newspaper about it and carried both away. Observe the decisive point, Watson. The outer leaves have met the rain, yet those within are untouched. The ticket must therefore have entered the fold before the paper was exposed to the weather. There was no theft, only a moment’s inattention.”

I found Miss Bell a cab, and she reached Euston in good time for the six forty.

On my return Holmes was again upon the sofa.

“A case without a culprit,” I remarked.

“My dear Watson,” said he, closing his eyes, “error requires none.”

No crime had been done; no furtive hand had meddled with her property. The matter was, in truth, no more than one of those small domestic mishaps which torment the victim out of all measure to their real importance. Yet Holmes brought to it the same cold attention which he might have given to the darkest intrigue.

It was shortly after five upon a raw November evening. Rain rattled against the panes of our Baker Street room, and the lamps below glimmered through the wet dusk like blurred yellow stars. Holmes had stretched his spare length upon the sofa, while I sat beside the fire, until our landlady admitted a young lady whose pale face and hurried breathing betrayed an anxiety which her firm voice sought in vain to conceal.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

Her cloak shone with rain. Beneath her left arm she carried a folded newspaper, its outer sheets sodden and discoloured.

Holmes raised himself upon one elbow.

“You last saw the ticket?”

“This morning in my purse. I am nearly sure that it was still there at luncheon.”

At his request she emptied the purse upon our table. A few coins, two keys, a lace handkerchief, and several crumpled receipts formed its entire contents. I examined the pockets and lining with care, but discovered nothing.

“Your movements since luncheon?” asked Holmes.

“And you noticed the loss twenty minutes ago?”

“Yes. Can someone have stolen it?”

“No.”

The quiet certainty of his reply astonished me. He had touched neither her cloak nor her purse. Instead, he stepped to her chair and lifted the newspaper. Drops stood upon its exposed fold, and a little pool had gathered beneath it.

“You bought this near the tea-room?”

“Just outside. I read it over tea, folded it before leaving, and held it under my arm.”

Holmes opened the paper. The wet outer leaves adhered with a soft, pulpy sound, but the sheets within, as I could plainly see, were perfectly dry.

His keen face brightened.

“The ticket is inside your newspaper, Miss Bell.”

He gave the folded pages a brisk shake. Out fluttered the missing return ticket, settling upon the hearthrug.

Our visitor gazed from it to Holmes in delighted amazement.

Miss Bell thanked him with much warmth, and I found her a cab in good time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

“Most lost things, Watson,” said Holmes, settling once more upon the sofa, “have merely been put somewhere.”

Holmes was stretched upon the sofa, his gaunt hands clasped over one knee, while I stirred the fire. Our landlady entered with a young woman close behind her.

“My return railway ticket is missing, Mr Holmes. My train departs from Euston at six-forty.”

“In my purse this morning. I think it was still there at luncheon.”

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, then took tea nearby. After that I walked for some distance before hiring a cab to Baker Street.”

“And the loss became known to you?”

“About twenty minutes ago. Can it have been stolen?”

“You had the ticket earlier?”

“It was in my purse this morning. I believe I saw it again at luncheon.”

There was no theft, no culprit, and indeed no crime of any sort. Yet, for one wet hour in London, the loss had all the urgency of a graver mystery.

It was shortly after five on a November evening, and rain rattled upon the panes of our Baker Street room. Holmes had stretched his spare form upon the sofa, while I sat by the fire with a medical journal, whose author had contrived to make even fever tedious. Our landlady entered with a young lady close behind her.

“My name is Clara Bell,” said our visitor. “I must leave Euston by the six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

She spoke with admirable restraint, though her colour was high and her breath hurried. Her cloak shone with rain. Beneath her arm she carried a folded newspaper, sodden at the edges and stained to a deeper grey along its outer sheet.

Holmes glanced at the clock.

“Where did you last see the ticket?”

“In my purse this morning. I think I saw it there at luncheon also.”

At his request she emptied the purse upon our table. Out fell coins, keys, two bills, a handkerchief, and a small confusion of trifles. I examined the pockets and lining, then searched her gloves and card-case. The ticket was not among them.

“Your movements since luncheon?” asked Holmes.

“I went to a bookseller in the Strand, then to a tea-room. After that I walked for some distance and took a cab here.”

“And this paper?”

“I bought it outside the tea-room. I read it over my tea, folded it before going out, and have carried it under my arm ever since.”

“Do you believe,” she added, “that someone took the ticket?”

“No one took it,” said Holmes. “There has been no theft.”

His certainty amazed me, for he had scarcely moved from the sofa. Now, however, he rose and held out one thin hand for the newspaper. Drops stood upon its exposed fold, and the outer leaves adhered in a clammy mass. He opened it with care. The inner pages parted crisply.

They were dry.

Holmes gave the quick, keen smile which I knew so well.

“Your ticket is inside the folded newspaper, Miss Bell.”

He turned the sheets over, and the missing return ticket slipped from between them to the hearth-rug.

Clara Bell uttered a little cry of relief.

It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men’s motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results. Grit in a sensitive instrument, or a crack in one of his own high-power lenses, would not be more disturbing than a strong emotion in a nature such as his. And yet there was but one woman to him, and that woman was the late Irene Adler, of dubious and questionable memory.

I had seen little of Holmes lately. My marriage had drifted us away from each other. My own complete happiness, and the home-centred interests which rise up around the man who first finds himself master of his own establishment, were sufficient to absorb all my attention, while Holmes, who loathed every form of society with his whole Bohemian soul, remained in our lodgings in Baker Street, buried among his old books, and alternating from week to week between cocaine and ambition, the drowsiness of the drug, and the fierce energy of his own keen nature. He was still, as ever, deeply attracted by the study of crime, and occupied his immense faculties and extraordinary powers of observation in following out those clues, and clearing up those mysteries which had been abandoned as hopeless by the official police. From time to time I heard some vague account of his doings: of his summons to Odessa in the case of the Trepoff murder, of his clearing up of the singular tragedy of the Atkinson brothers at Trincomalee, and finally of the mission which he had accomplished so delicately and successfully for the reigning family of Holland. Beyond these signs of his activity, however, which I merely shared with all the readers of the daily press, I knew little of my former friend and companion.

One night—it was on the twentieth of March, 1888—I was returning from a journey to a patient (for I had now returned to civil practice), when my way led me through Baker Street. As I passed the well-remembered door, which must always be associated in my mind with my wooing, and with the dark incidents of the Study in Scarlet, I was seized with a keen desire to see Holmes again, and to know how he was employing his extraordinary powers. His rooms were brilliantly lit, and, even as I looked up, I saw his tall, spare figure pass twice in a dark silhouette against the blind. He was pacing the room swiftly, eagerly, with his head sunk upon his chest and his hands clasped behind him. To me, who knew his every mood and habit, his attitude and manner told their own story. He was at work again. He had risen out of his drug-created dreams and was hot upon the scent of some new problem. I rang the bell and was shown up to the chamber which had formerly been in part my own.

---

“My dear fellow,” said Sherlock Holmes as we sat on either side of the fire in his lodgings at Baker Street, “life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence. If we could fly out of that window hand in hand, hover over this great city, gently remove the roofs, and peep in at the queer things which are going on, the strange coincidences, the plannings, the cross-purposes, the wonderful chains of events, working through generations, and leading to the most _outré_ results, it would make all fiction with its conventionalities and foreseen conclusions most stale and unprofitable.”

“And yet I am not convinced of it,” I answered. “The cases which come to light in the papers are, as a rule, bald enough, and vulgar enough. We have in our police reports realism pushed to its extreme limits, and yet the result is, it must be confessed, neither fascinating nor artistic.”

“A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect,” remarked Holmes. “This is wanting in the police report, where more stress is laid, perhaps, upon the platitudes of the magistrate than upon the details, which to an observer contain the vital essence of the whole matter. Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.”

I smiled and shook my head. “I can quite understand your thinking so,” I said. “Of course, in your position of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled, throughout three continents, you are brought in contact with all that is strange and bizarre. But here”—I picked up the morning paper from the ground—“let us put it to a practical test. Here is the first heading upon which I come. ‘A husband’s cruelty to his wife.’ There is half a column of print, but I know without reading it that it is all perfectly familiar to me. There is, of course, the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, the sympathetic sister or landlady. The crudest of writers could invent nothing more crude.”

“Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument,” said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. “This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.”

He held out his snuffbox of old gold, with a great amethyst in the centre of the lid. Its splendour was in such contrast to his homely ways and simple life that I could not help commenting upon it.

---

When I glance over my notes and records of the Sherlock Holmes cases between the years ’82 and ’90, I am faced by so many which present strange and interesting features that it is no easy matter to know which to choose and which to leave. Some, however, have already gained publicity through the papers, and others have not offered a field for those peculiar qualities which my friend possessed in so high a degree, and which it is the object of these papers to illustrate. Some, too, have baffled his analytical skill, and would be, as narratives, beginnings without an ending, while others have been but partially cleared up, and have their explanations founded rather upon conjecture and surmise than on that absolute logical proof which was so dear to him. There is, however, one of these last which was so remarkable in its details and so startling in its results that I am tempted to give some account of it in spite of the fact that there are points in connection with it which never have been, and probably never will be, entirely cleared up.

The year ’87 furnished us with a long series of cases of greater or less interest, of which I retain the records. Among my headings under this one twelve months I find an account of the adventure of the Paradol Chamber, of the Amateur Mendicant Society, who held a luxurious club in the lower vault of a furniture warehouse, of the facts connected with the loss of the British barque _Sophy Anderson_, of the singular adventures of the Grice Patersons in the island of Uffa, and finally of the Camberwell poisoning case. In the latter, as may be remembered, Sherlock Holmes was able, by winding up the dead man’s watch, to prove that it had been wound up two hours before, and that therefore the deceased had gone to bed within that time—a deduction which was of the greatest importance in clearing up the case. All these I may sketch out at some future date, but none of them present such singular features as the strange train of circumstances which I have now taken up my pen to describe.

It was in the latter days of September, and the equinoctial gales had set in with exceptional violence. All day the wind had screamed and the rain had beaten against the windows, so that even here in the heart of great, hand-made London we were forced to raise our minds for the instant from the routine of life and to recognise the presence of those great elemental forces which shriek at mankind through the bars of his civilisation, like untamed beasts in a cage. As evening drew in, the storm grew higher and louder, and the wind cried and sobbed like a child in the chimney. Sherlock Holmes sat moodily at one side of the fireplace cross-indexing his records of crime, while I at the other was deep in one of Clark Russell’s fine sea-stories until the howl of the gale from without seemed to blend with the text, and the splash of the rain to lengthen out into the long swash of the sea waves. My wife was on a visit to her mother’s, and for a few days I was a dweller once more in my old quarters at Baker Street.

“You last saw the ticket where?”

“In my purse this morning. I am almost sure that it was still there at luncheon.”

“Yes. I laid it open beside my purse, folded it before leaving, and carried it under my arm.”

Holmes parted the wet outer pages. The deeper leaves separated with a faint, crisp rustle.

“Observe, Watson. The newspaper’s interior is dry.”

“Three times. Could a thief have taken it?”

He studied the blackened outer fold, upon which water stood in beads. Then he opened the sheets. They resisted him at first, being damp along the exposed margins; but the inner pages parted with a crisp rustle. Their surface was unmarked by rain. The newspaper’s interior was dry.

Holmes gave the brief, keen smile which announced that the matter was finished.

“My return railway ticket is missing, Mr Holmes,” she began. “My train departs from Euston at six forty. I have searched everywhere.”

“Not everywhere, I think,” said Holmes. “But let us proceed in order. Where did you last see it?”

“In my purse this morning. I am nearly certain that it was still there at luncheon.”

At Holmes’s request she poured the contents of the purse upon our table. Coins, keys, receipts, and a small handkerchief lay in a confused heap. I examined the pockets and lining, but found no trace of the ticket.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, and then walked until the rain forced me to hire a cab.”

“You bought the newspaper before taking tea?”

“Yes. I read it there, folded it as I left, and carried it under my arm.”

Her voice faltered.

“Could anyone have stolen the ticket?”

“No one has stolen it,” said Holmes.

There was no theft, nor had any culprit a part in it. The matter was no more than a mishap; yet Holmes brought to it that exact gaze which had pierced mysteries of a far darker sort.

Rain had fallen since noon, and by six o’clock Baker Street lay blurred behind streaming panes. I had drawn my chair close to the fire, while Holmes, stretched upon the sofa, watched the smoke of his cigarette curl towards the ceiling. A hurried step sounded upon the stair, and a moment later Clara Bell entered our room.

“Mr Holmes,” she cried, “my return railway ticket is gone, and my train departs from Euston at six-forty.”

“That gives us little time,” said Holmes. “Pray tell me where you last saw it.”

“In my purse this morning. I may have seen it again at luncheon, though I cannot be sure.”

At Holmes’s request she emptied the purse upon our table. I examined the coins, receipts, keys, and handkerchief, and even ran my finger along the lining. The ticket was not there.

“Your movements since luncheon?” Holmes asked.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, and walked for some distance before finding a cab.”

“And you fear a thief?”

“I can think of nothing else.”

“You may dismiss that fear,” said Holmes. “No one has robbed you.”

He shook out the folded sheets, and the missing return ticket fluttered upon the hearth-rug.

Our client stared at him in delighted bewilderment.

“You removed it from your purse in the tea-room,” Holmes explained, “most probably when searching for money, and placed it between the open pages without thought. Then you folded the newspaper and went into the rain. Consider, Watson: the outside is saturated, while the interior remains dry. Anything now enclosed within those inner leaves must have entered before the paper was exposed to the weather.”

Miss Bell thanked him warmly, and I secured a cab which allowed her ample time to reach Euston for the six-forty.

When I returned, Holmes had resumed his place upon the sofa.

“A mystery without a villain,” said I.

“The commonest kind, Watson—and sometimes the neatest.”

Among the lesser puzzles which came before Sherlock Holmes, I can recall none that showed more neatly the worth of a single plain fact than the affair of Miss Clara Bell’s return railway ticket. There was no theft, nor any culprit to pursue. Indeed, the matter was so slight that another man might have dismissed it with a shrug; yet it gave me a fresh glimpse of that exact method by which Holmes drew certainty from trifles.

Rain was beating upon the windows of our Baker Street rooms one November evening, and the lamps below showed as blurred yellow stains through the streaming panes. Holmes reclined upon the sofa, lean and silent, while I sat beside the fire with a medical journal. A hurried step sounded upon the stair, and our visitor entered.

She was a young woman of quiet dress and troubled eyes.

“I am Clara Bell,” said she. “My train departs from Euston at six-forty, and my return railway ticket is missing.”

Her cloak sparkled with rain. Beneath her arm she held a folded newspaper, whose exposed sheets were sodden and limp.

Holmes glanced at the clock. “You last saw the ticket?”

“In my purse this morning. I think it was still there at luncheon.”

She emptied the purse upon our table. Coins, keys, receipts, and a lace handkerchief lay before us. I examined every scrap, then searched the purse itself, even pressing the worn lining between finger and thumb. The ticket was not there.

“Your movements since luncheon?” asked Holmes.

“I visited a bookseller in the Strand, took tea nearby, walked for some way, and then came here by cab.”

“Did anyone approach you?”

“No one that I noticed. But surely it may have been stolen.”

“There has been no theft,” said Holmes.

His tone carried such calm conviction that Miss Bell ceased at once to question him. For my own part, I could see no ground for it. He had scarcely looked at the purse and had not stirred from the sofa.

At last he rose and took the newspaper from her. A drop slid from its lower edge to the carpet.

“You bought this before taking tea?”

“Yes. I read it at the table, folded it before going out, and kept it under my arm through the rain.”

Holmes parted the wet outer pages. The inner leaves opened with a crisp rustle.

“Observe, Watson.”

The newspaper’s interior was dry.

His keen face brightened. He turned the folded paper over and gave it one sharp shake. From between the sheltered sheets a small buff ticket fluttered down upon the hearthrug.

Clara Bell gave a cry of relief.

“You took it from your purse at the tearoom,” said Holmes, “perhaps while seeking a coin, and slipped it between the open pages without thought. You then folded the newspaper indoors. The rain soaked only the exposed part. Since the interior remains dry, the ticket must have been enclosed before you stepped into the street.”

I found Miss Bell a cab, and she reached Euston in ample time for the six-forty.

“A case without a villain,” I remarked upon my return.

Holmes settled back among the cushions. “Most lost things, my dear Watson, require observation—not justice.”
